title: Research papers
summary: These papers study how abelian Galois data detect automorphisms and how the geometry of a boundary controls finite covers over the integers.
overview: This collection develops selected results from three papers on Galois groups and coverings over the integers. The first asks whether finite Galois automorphisms can be distinguished through their actions on abelian quotients, and proves this form of faithfulness for discretely valued fields of mixed characteristic and for higher local fields of positive dimension.

The second explains when removing a horizontal divisor leaves solvable covering theory unchanged. Under its arithmetic boundary condition, it also reduces the extension of a representation across the divisor to the same question for its reduction modulo the maximal ideal.

The third studies complements of rational sections of the projective line. Determinant valuations measure intersections and detect configurations that force a connected double cover, including every configuration with at least seven sections. These results establish that quadratic obstruction; the paper's full equivalence between normal crossings at two and prosolvable triviality is not yet part of the selection.
scopeNote: These are selected completed declarations, not a claim that all three papers are completely formalized. In particular, the general Hilbertian application still needs its embedding-problem input; several examples in the solvable-coverings paper remain outside scope; and the full normal-crossings/prosolvable-triviality equivalence in Theorem 2.6 of the branched-coverings paper is not claimed here. The large-boundary entry covers only the at-least-seven case of Corollary 2.7.

entries.title: Ab-faithfulness
entries.summary: Finite relative quotients must be detectable by their action on abelianized open normal subgroups.
statement: A profinite group $G$ is ab-faithful if, for every open subgroup $H\le G$ and every open normal subgroup $N\triangleleft H$, the conjugation action gives an injection
$$H/N\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}(N^{\mathrm{ab}}),\qquad N^{\mathrm{ab}}=N/\overline{[N,N]}.$$
For a set of primes $\Sigma$, the $\Sigma$-version replaces $N^{\mathrm{ab}}$ by $(N^\Sigma)^{\mathrm{ab}}$, where $N^\Sigma$ is the maximal pro-$\Sigma$ quotient.
discussion: For absolute Galois groups, the condition tests relative automorphisms through the abelian Galois theory of finite extensions. Information from many extensions can therefore retain structure lost by abelianizing the original group alone. Yamaguchi's 2026 paper introduces the prime-restricted form in Definition 1.1 and uses valuation theory and embedding problems to establish the property and connect it with center-freeness and slimness.
history: Yamaguchi's 2026 paper places ab-faithfulness in the study of absolute Galois groups and finite-step solvable quotients. Definition 1.1 gives the prime-restricted form. The paper then develops valuation-theoretic and embedding-problem methods for establishing the property, and relates it to questions of center-freeness and slimness.

entries.title: Mixed-characteristic discrete valuations
entries.summary: Conjugation on the mod-p abelianized absolute Galois group detects every element of a finite Galois group.
statement: Let $K$ have characteristic $0$ and a discrete valuation with residue characteristic $p>0$. For every finite Galois extension $L/K$,
$$\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}(G_L^{\mathrm{ab}}/p)$$
is injective. In addition, $G_K$ is $p$-ab-faithful. Neither completeness nor Henselianity of the given valuation is assumed in this declaration.
discussion: The field need only carry a discrete valuation of mixed characteristic $(0,p)$; completeness and Henselianity are unnecessary. Detection through a single prime thus applies beyond ordinary local fields. Yamaguchi's Theorem 3.6 proves this using Kummer theory and a reduction to prime-degree extensions, providing an input to the higher-local-field theorem and later applications to solvable Galois quotients.
history: This is Theorem 3.6 of Yamaguchi's 2026 ab-faithfulness paper. Its mixed-characteristic argument uses Kummer theory and a reduction to prime-degree extensions. Within the paper, this valuation-theoretic result supplies an important input for the higher-local-field theorem and subsequent applications to solvable quotients.

entries.title: Higher local fields
entries.summary: Every positive-dimensional higher local field has an ab-faithful absolute Galois group.
statement: An $n$-dimensional higher local field is defined recursively: dimension $0$ means a finite field, and dimension $n+1$ means a field with a complete discrete valuation whose residue field is $n$-dimensional. The theorem states
$$n>0,\quad K\text{ an }n\text{-dimensional higher local field}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad G_K\text{ is ab-faithful}.$$
discussion: Higher local fields are built through successive complete discrete valuations ending in a finite residue field. The uniform conclusion over finite extensions is useful for studying solvable quotients, where conjugation must remain controlled after passing to open subgroups. Yamaguchi's Theorem 4.2 follows the residue-field towers, combining mixed-characteristic detection with lifting from characteristic-zero residue fields.
history: Theorem 4.2 of Yamaguchi's 2026 paper extends the ab-faithfulness discussion to positive-dimensional higher local fields. The argument follows their residue-field towers, combining mixed-characteristic detection with lifting from characteristic-zero residue fields. The paper then uses these examples in its study of finite-step solvable Galois groups.

entries.title: The étale fundamental group of Spec Z
entries.summary: Every geometric base point gives the trivial étale fundamental group of the integers.
statement: For a separably closed field $\Omega$ and any geometric point $\xi:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z$,
$$\pi_1^{\mathrm{\acute et}}(\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z,\xi)=1.$$
The Lean conclusion is that the automorphism group of the geometric fiber functor is a subsingleton.
discussion: In number-field terms, every nontrivial finite extension of $\mathbb Q$ ramifies at some finite prime. This rigidity gives a base case for arguments over the integers: extending a covering across all possible boundary can force it to be trivial. The classical proof uses Minkowski's discriminant theorem; Yamaguchi records it as Example 1.4(1), with SGA 1 providing the language of finite étale covers and fundamental groups.
history: The classical argument uses Minkowski's discriminant theorem to exclude nontrivial number fields unramified at every finite prime. Yamaguchi records the result as Example 1.4(1). SGA 1 supplies the language that expresses the absence of such connected covers as triviality of an étale fundamental group.

entries.title: The arithmetic boundary condition
entries.summary: A local condition at characteristic two is combined with a geometric-integrality condition that survives every connected finite étale cover.
statement: Let $X$ be connected and locally Noetherian, and let $D$ be a horizontal effective Cartier divisor: each prime component dominates $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z$. Condition $(\dagger)$ requires all three of the following.

The scheme $X$ is regular along $D$. Every prime component of $D$ contains a residue-characteristic-$2$ point where $D$ has normal crossings. After every connected finite étale cover $X'\to X$, each reduced prime component of the pulled-back boundary has geometrically integral generic fiber over $\mathbb Q$.
discussion: Persistence after finite étale base change lets the same abelian argument be applied to open subgroups of the fundamental group. This is the mechanism for reaching conclusions about all solvable coverings. Definition 2.2 of Yamaguchi's 2026 paper introduces the condition after an abelian invariance result and explains why geometric integrality of the original boundary alone does not suffice.
history: Definition 2.2 of Yamaguchi's 2026 solvable-coverings paper introduces this condition after an abelian invariance result. The paper explains why geometric integrality of the original boundary alone is insufficient: it must remain available after finite étale base change to support the stronger prosolvable conclusion.

entries.title: A perfect boundary kernel
entries.summary: Under the arithmetic boundary condition, removing the divisor does not change the maximal prosolvable fundamental group.
statement: Let $X$ be connected and locally Noetherian, and let $D$ be a horizontal effective Cartier divisor. Assume condition $(\dagger)$: $X$ is regular along $D$; each prime component contains a characteristic-$2$ normal-crossings point of $D$; and each reduced boundary component has geometrically integral generic fiber over $\mathbb Q$ after every connected finite étale cover of $X$. Put $U=X\setminus D$. The theorem proves that $U$ is connected. For a geometric point $\xi$ of $U$, let
$$f:\pi_1^{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\xi)\longrightarrow\pi_1^{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X,\xi),\qquad K=\ker(f).$$
Then $K=\overline{[K,K]}$, with closure taken in $K$, and the inclusion-induced map gives
$$\pi_1^{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U,\xi)^{\mathrm{solv}}\xrightarrow{\sim}\pi_1^{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X,\xi)^{\mathrm{solv}}.$$
discussion: The kernel created in the full fundamental group is topologically perfect, so finite solvable quotients cannot detect it. This explains how the boundary can retain nonabelian information without producing new solvable covers. Yamaguchi's Theorem 2.5 obtains this stronger conclusion by applying the abelian invariance argument after finite étale covers; the perfect-kernel formulation also leads to the subsequent representation-extension result.
history: This is Theorem 2.5 of Yamaguchi's 2026 paper on extending solvable coverings. It advances from abelian invariance to prosolvable invariance by applying the abelian argument after finite étale covers. The formulation through a perfect kernel also prepares the representation-extension result that follows.

entries.title: Extending a representation from its reduction
entries.summary: A continuous representation extends across the boundary exactly when its residue representation does.
statement: Let $X$ be connected and locally Noetherian, and let $D$ be a horizontal effective Cartier divisor. Assume $X$ is regular along $D$, each prime component contains a characteristic-$2$ normal-crossings point of $D$, and all reduced boundary components have geometrically integral generic fibers over $\mathbb Q$ after every connected finite étale cover of $X$. Put $U=X\setminus D$. Let $A$ be a complete Noetherian local ring with finite residue field $k_A$ of characteristic $p$, carrying its maximal-ideal-adic topology. For $n\ge1$ and a continuous representation $\rho:\pi_1^{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U)\to\mathrm{GL}_n(A)$,
$$\rho\text{ factors continuously through }\pi_1^{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\bar\rho\text{ does}.$$
Here $\bar\rho$ is reduction modulo the maximal ideal, with the discrete topology on $k_A$. When the factorization of $\rho$ exists, it is unique.
discussion: The extension problem over a complete Noetherian local ring with finite residue field becomes a question over finite coefficients. A perfect boundary kernel contributes no obstruction through the successive abelian pieces of the congruence filtration, so the residual test suffices at every adic level. Corollary 2.6 of Yamaguchi's 2026 paper applies the preceding perfect-kernel theorem in exactly this way.
history: Corollary 2.6 of Yamaguchi's 2026 solvable-coverings paper follows the perfect-kernel theorem. It applies that geometric result to continuous linear representations, using the congruence filtration of a complete local coefficient ring. The conclusion connects extension of arithmetic coverings with reduction modulo the maximal ideal.

entries.title: Normal crossings from rational sections
entries.summary: Normal crossings can be tested by counting colliding sections and measuring the valuation of their determinants.
statement: Let $A\subset\mathbb P^1(\mathbb Q)$ be finite, and let $D_A$ be the divisor formed by the integral sections corresponding to its points. For primitive coordinates $a=[u_a:v_a]$ and $b=[u_b:v_b]$, put $\Delta(a,b)=u_av_b-u_bv_a$, up to the harmless sign of the chosen primitive representatives.

For a prime $p$, the divisor $(D_A)_{\mathbb Z_p}$ has normal crossings if and only if every closed point of $\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb F_p}$ lies on at most two labelled sections and every distinct pair meeting there satisfies
$$v_p\!\left(\Delta(a,b)\right)=1.$$
discussion: At most two sections may meet at a point of the special fiber, and each meeting pair must have determinant valuation one. These tests retain the identities of sections that coincide after reduction, turning local geometry into explicit arithmetic. Lemma 2.3 of Shimizu and Yamaguchi's 2026 paper develops this criterion as input to the study of dyadic collisions and finite quotients of the complement's fundamental group.
history: Lemma 2.3 of Shimizu and Yamaguchi's 2026 paper develops this criterion for rational sections of the projective line over the integers. It supplies the local arithmetic input for the later analysis of dyadic collisions and finite quotients of the complement's fundamental group.

entries.title: Intersection multiplicity as a determinant valuation
entries.summary: The local intersection length of two rational sections is exactly the p-adic valuation of their determinant.
statement: Let $a\ne b$ be rational points of $\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb Q}$, with associated sections $D_a,D_b\subset\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb Z}$. Let $y$ be a point of the fiber over a prime $p$ lying on $D_b$, and let $x$ be its image in $\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb Z}$. Then
$$\operatorname{length}_{\mathcal O_x}\!\left(\mathcal O_x/(I_a+I_b)_x\right)=v_p\!\left(\Delta(a,b)\right).$$
discussion: Divisibility records the order of contact, as well as whether two sections meet modulo a prime. Valuation one gives a transverse intersection, while larger valuations detect higher multiplicity. This is the intersection-multiplicity part of Lemma 2.3 in Shimizu–Yamaguchi, where the local-length interpretation connects rational coordinates with the geometry of arithmetic surfaces and supports the normal-crossings criterion.
history: This is the intersection-multiplicity component of Lemma 2.3 in Shimizu–Yamaguchi. The paper uses the local-length interpretation of the determinant valuation to connect explicit rational coordinates with the geometry of arithmetic surfaces.

entries.title: A quadratic quotient from failure at 2
entries.summary: Failure of normal crossings over the 2-adic integers produces a nontrivial quotient of the actual arithmetic fundamental group.
statement: For finite $A\subset\mathbb P^1(\mathbb Q)$, put $U_A=\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb Z}\setminus D_A$. If $(D_A)_{\mathbb Z_2}$ is not a normal-crossings divisor, then for every geometric point $\xi$ of $U_A$ there is a continuous surjection
$$\pi_1^{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U_A,\xi)\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z.$$
discussion: The quotient has order two, so the integral complement admits a connected double cover and its maximal prosolvable fundamental group is nontrivial. A local defect at one prime thus obstructs global triviality of solvable covering theory. Proposition 2.5 of Shimizu–Yamaguchi constructs this quadratic obstruction; it establishes one direction of the relation with normal crossings at two, while the converse requires further arguments.
history: Proposition 2.5 of Shimizu–Yamaguchi constructs this quadratic obstruction. It supplies one direction of the paper's relation between normal crossings at two and solvable quotients. The opposite direction requires further arguments; the quadratic construction alone does not establish the full equivalence.

entries.title: At least seven sections force a quotient
entries.summary: The complement of seven or more distinct rational sections always has a cyclic quotient of order two.
statement: Let $A\subset\mathbb P^1(\mathbb Q)$ be finite with $|A|\ge7$, and form the open complement $U_A\subset\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb Z}$ of the corresponding integral sections. For every geometric point $\xi$ of $U_A$,
$$\exists\,\phi:\pi_1^{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U_A,\xi)\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\quad\text{continuous}.$$
discussion: Only three rational reduction points are available over $\mathbb F_2$, and normal crossings permits at most two sections through each. Seven sections therefore force a collision that produces a connected double cover, giving an obstruction determined solely by the boundary count. This is the large-boundary case of Corollary 2.7 in Shimizu–Yamaguchi, whose threshold comes from that six-section bound.
history: This is the large-boundary case of Corollary 2.7 in Shimizu–Yamaguchi. The paper observes that normal crossings at two permits at most two sections through each of the three rational points of the dyadic projective line, giving the threshold of six.
